headline: Medium risk: Haystack can ingest and forward content via MCP/REST, while Marker is local-only, creating prompt-injection and cascading-error exposure but limited direct leakage.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Haystack exposes MCP servers and REST APIs, so it can ingest external content and pass it onward; Marker has no MCP and no filesystem write, but if its outputs are fed into Haystack or vice versa, instruction-like text can be misread. The pair lacks a documented isolation boundary, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF Haystack ingests Marker-produced text as trusted instructions
IF a shared MCP or REST bridge forwards untrusted document content between the agents
mitigations: Disable MCP endpoints not needed for the workflow
Wrap inter-agent messages in a strict schema with instruction/content separation
Add a provenance tag to all Marker outputs before Haystack consumes them
Require human review for any prompt-like text extracted from documents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Haystack has broad network egress, but its touched data class is only anonymous usage statistics in the profile; Marker has no network egress and no filesystem read/write, so there is no clear default path for sensitive data exfiltration between them. The main risk is limited to accidental forwarding of whatever Haystack already receives.
conditions: IF Haystack is configured to process sensitive documents
IF Marker outputs are routed into Haystack and then sent over the network
mitigations: Keep sensitive inputs out of Haystack unless necessary
Turn off external connectors for Haystack where possible
Use a local-only deployment path for both agents
Log and review outbound requests from Haystack for unexpected payloads

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Haystack can use MCP and network egress, while Marker cannot write files, modify git state, or spawn subprocesses. That means overlapping mutable-resource conflict is not evident from the profiles; only indirect coordination issues remain, so the blast radius is small and the pathway is weak.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same external API or MCP resource
IF an orchestrator gives Marker write access not shown in the profile
mitigations: Assign separate credentials per agent
Avoid shared mutable backends unless locking exists
Keep Marker in read-only mode
Document which agent owns each external resource

D_cascading_error.rationale: Haystack is a search-RAG agent and Marker is a document-processing agent, so a plausible pipeline is Marker output feeding Haystack retrieval or generation. If Haystack treats that output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream answers or actions. No verification mechanism is documented, so uncertainty favors medium.
conditions: IF Marker output is used as Haystack input without a verification step
IF Haystack-generated claims are reused downstream as facts
mitigations: Insert a validation step between Marker and Haystack
Require citations or source spans for any extracted claim
Flag low-confidence extractions before retrieval indexing
Have a human approve high-impact outputs before action

E_compliance.rationale: The profiles do not show regulated data classes, residency constraints, or retention mismatches. Haystack touches anonymous usage statistics and Marker lists no data classes, so there is no documented compliance conflict to score for this pair. The absence of a cited mismatch keeps this at none.
conditions: IF either profile later adds regulated data classes such as PHI or EU PII
IF residency or retention policies are introduced for shared data
mitigations: Confirm data-class handling before deployment
Record retention settings for each agent
Separate regulated workloads from this pair
Review vendor terms if new compliance scopes are added
